newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian stocks poised for lacklustre week.
newsitem.headline: Asian stocks poised for lacklustre week.

text.p: Asian stocks are due for another lacklustre week with the usual exception of Hong Kong, which is set to maintain its stellar pace, brokers said.

Disappointing economic fundamentals are expected to continue to weigh on most southeast Asian markets, but optimism about the July 1 handover to China will continue to spur Hong Kong stocks on to new highs, they said.
Australia and New Zealand should also make some gains, while Tokyo caps recent strength at the key barrier of 20,000.

TOKYO - The Tokyo stock market's key index is likely to stall around the key 20,000 line in the week ahead, with export-oriented stocks lacking the impetus to fuel a further rally due to the yen's uncertain outlook, brokers say.
"Many people will opt to sell stocks on a Nikkei rally above 20,000," said Kiyoshi Kimura, general manager of research at Societe Generale Securities.
Lingering worries about the recent rise of the yen have clipped the wings of leading exporters, which had pulled the whole market higher in previous rallies this year and last.
On Friday, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,068.81, up 59.81 points, or 0.27 percent, from its close on May 23.
- - - - HONG KONG - Hong Kong stocks are expected to
continue their drive into record ground this week, although analysts said some consolidation could set in before the Hang Seng Index challenges its next target at 15,000 points.

"There is no question that this market is in a strong upswing," said Howard Gorges, vice chairman at South China Holdings. "15,000 is certainly near at hand but I expect that there might be some breather."
The Hang Seng Index surged 426.13 points, or 2.97 percent, last week to close at an all-time high of 14,757.81 on Friday.
BANGKOK - The Thai stock market is expected to decline slightly as investors stay on the sidelines.

However, traders said that with the resumption of trade in troubled finance house, Finance One, and Thursday's battery of economic data behind them, some investors could dip into the market to pick up bargain shares.

Brokers said they would be watching to see how effective housing loans of about 17 billion baht, which are to be offered by two government-run banks to the public from Monday, would assist the ailing property sector.
The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index rose 1.47 percent on Friday to end at 566.39 points, trimming the week's loss to 2.54 percent.
DHAKA - Stock prices in Bangladesh are expected to continue their rally in the week beginning on Sunday with fresh investor commitments ahead of the national budget, brokers said.

The upbeat mood will prevail ahead of the budget due on June 12 and following the recent reorganisation of the governing council of the Dhaka Stock Exchange, they said. The DSE benchmark index gained 28.84 points at 1,216.68 in the week to Thursday. Bangladesh has now introduced a two-day weekend on Friday and Saturday.
- - - - MANILA - Manila shares will likely suffer their
first setback this week as seven consecutive days of gains usher in profit-taking, traders said.
BPI Securities Corp analyst Spencer Yap said he expects the market to pull back with support at 2,600 to 2,650 points.
He said weak volumes indicate that foreign investors are still reticent about the market and are possibly awaiting the next spate of corporate earnings data.
The main index closed rose 211.25 points, or 7.52 percent, on the week to 2,809.45.
SEOUL - Seoul stocks would consolidate briefly and then continue to climb as investors bet on an economic turnaround and declining interest rates, brokers said.

"I'm sure the market is riding a bull-run," said Chung Dong-bae, market strategist at Daewoo Securities. "The index will rise to the 800 level in June. After a consolidation, it will head for the 900 mark this year."
Economists said economic indicators released on Friday showed the beleaguered economy was nearing bottom.

South Korea's consumer price index rose 3.8 percent in May on the year, down from a 5.1 percent rise a year earlier, while industrial output surged 10.7 percent in April, compared to an 8.4 percent rise a year earlier.
The composite index stood at 756.77 points at the close of Saturday's half-day trading session, up 31.6 points or 4.35 percent, from the previous Saturday.
Yields on benchmark three-year corporate bonds ended on Saturday at 11.90 percent, down from 12.15 a week earlier.
SINGAPORE - Singapore share prices are seen inching up this week, although punters and other market players will be looking for direction in early trade, brokers said.
"The market has already corrected. I think the general trend should be upwards," a broker for an investment house said.
One trader said there may be some uncertainty in the market coming out of the weekend.
The key Strait Times Industrial index closed on Friday at 2,065.48 points, up 10.12 points from the previous Friday's close of 2,055.36. - - - -
SYDNEY - Australian shares look set to continue their steep upward trajectory after finishing last week in record-breaking form with healthy buying interest apparent.
The All Ordinaries index ended up 0.8 percent at 2,610.5 on the day and up 1.8 percent for the week, having touched successive record highs, peaking on Friday at 2,617.4.
Brokers were confident the uptrend would stay intact with only a dramatic correction in the U.S. likely to slow buyers.
"I think our market would hold even if the Dow fell a 100 points or so," said Grant Williams of Reynolds.
TAIPEI - Taiwan share prices are expected to resume a downward consolidation, despite a sharp rebound on Saturday off recent malaise, brokers said.

The market, beset by political jitters and concerns over social disorder, has been mired in a low-turnover consolidation for more than a month, struggling to rekindle the kind of sustained rally seen earlier in the year.
"I don't think Saturday's gains will change the overall trend, because they were based mostly on technical grounds," said Oliver Fang, senior analyst for National Securities.
Electronic shares, boosted by sound fundamentals and recent correlative gains on Wall Street are expected to remain the market's heavy focus.
On Saturday, the benchmark stock index finished 1.98 percent or 158.62 points higher at 8,163.11, down slightly from 8,178.70 a week earlier.
A trading range of 7,800-8,250 is seen for next week, brokers said.
- - - - WELLINGTON - The New Zealand top-40 sharemarket
index ended the week 53.11 points higher than last Friday's close, with brokers seeing a continuation of the good tone on strong offshore interest in leading issues.

"The market is going through a better patch. There continues to be some good offshore interest in the leaders, and the quality second liners are being picked up by local investors," said Ord Minnett's director of equities John Rattray.
The NZSE-40 Capital Index closed the week at 2,356.80, up 53.11 points or 2.3 percent on last Friday's close.
